brand.title: IQVIA (Production)
brand.subtitle: Knowledge Check — Introduction to Social Selling Techniques

questions.question: Which two axes form the foundation of the Social Style Selling framework?
choices: Introvert vs. Extrovert and Thinking vs. Feeling
Ask vs. Tell and Task vs. People
Fast vs. Slow and Detail vs. Big Picture
Aggressive vs. Passive and Rational vs. Emotional
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—the X axis (Ask vs. Tell) and Y axis (Task vs. People) are the two core questions that determine where every style lands on the grid.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The framework is built on two simple questions: How does this person get what they want (Ask or Tell)? and What drives their behavior (Task or People)? These axes create the four-quadrant grid.

questions.question: Which of the following is a signature question that Drivers typically lead with?
choices: How does this work and how was it measured?
Why should we choose this solution and why now?
What are the results and what is the outcome?
Who else is using this and who should be involved?
questions.feedback_correct: Right—Drivers ask "What?" because they are focused on results and outcomes above all else.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not this one. Remember, each style has a signature question: Drivers ask "What?", Analyticals ask "How?", Amiables ask "Why?", and Expressives ask "Who?". The signature question is your clearest early signal of style.

questions.question: What do Amiables do when they feel pressured or when a conversation goes off track?
choices: They take control of the meeting
They ask for more time and more data
They go quiet and withdraw
They become argumentative
questions.feedback_correct: Correct—when an Amiable feels pressured, they withdraw and go quiet, which is their way of signaling that something has broken down in the relationship.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not that one. Each style has a different pressure behavior: Drivers take control, Analyticals ask for more data, Expressives get argumentative, and Amiables go quiet and withdraw. Amiables withdraw because they avoid conflict.

questions.question: What are the three diagnostic questions you should use to read a buyer's style in the first few minutes?
choices: Do they prefer email or phone, are they early or late to meetings, and do they ask follow-up questions?
Do they tell or ask, what do they focus on (results/data/relationships/vision), and how much emotion do they show?
How much do they talk, do they smile frequently, and how quickly do they make decisions?
Are they introverted or extroverted, do they think logically or emotionally, and how organized are they?
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—those three observable signals are all you need to place a buyer on the grid accurately in most first meetings.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The three diagnostic questions are: (1) Does this person tell or ask? (2) What do they focus on—results, data, relationships, or vision? (3) How much emotion do they show—low and controlled, or high and animated? These are behavioral observations, not personality categories.

questions.question: When selling to an Analytical buyer, what is the most important thing to avoid?
choices: Asking too many questions or taking up too much of their time
Being too formal or using overly technical language they won't understand
Getting personal or presenting in a sloppy, imprecise way
Offering too many options or giving them control over the next steps
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—Analyticals need to feel that your process is rigorous and thorough; getting personal or being sloppy damages rapport faster than almost anything else.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not that one. With Analyticals, the worst mistake is getting personal or being imprecise—they need to see a logical, well-documented process anchored in evidence and accuracy.

questions.question: What does an Expressive buyer most want to feel from a sales rep during discovery?
choices: That you have thoroughly researched their business and understand their data
That you respect their time and can deliver results quickly
That you understand them personally and are genuinely engaged and enthusiastic
That you will work collaboratively with them as a trusted partner
questions.feedback_correct: Yes—Expressives are animated and want to be heard and recognized; they read the room and notice if you are not genuinely engaged.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not that one. While Expressives value different things than other styles, they specifically need you to show enthusiasm and active engagement. They think in terms of vision and possibilities, and they want to feel that you are personally invested in their story.

questions.question: Your own Social Style as a sales rep can actually work against you when selling to buyers of a different style—true or false, and why?
choices: False, because your natural style is always an advantage regardless of who you are selling to
True, because the way you naturally communicate lands differently depending on the buyer's style, and a mismatch can shut down rapport
False, because all buyers respect confidence and authenticity above style matching
True, but only if you are an Analytical or Driver, since those styles are harder to relate to
questions.feedback_correct: Spot on—a Driver rep's direct, low-emotion approach works great for another Driver but can shut down an Amiable before the conversation starts. Awareness of your own defaults is step one.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Your natural style absolutely can work against you. For example, a Driver rep leading hard with conclusions and keeping emotion out can feel cold and transactional to an Amiable buyer. That mismatch is why versatility—adjusting to match the buyer—is a critical skill.

questions.question: What is the key difference between catching a style mismatch early versus late in a sales conversation?
choices: Early catching lets you shift before rapport is damaged; late catching means rebuilding trust you did not need to lose
Early catching is impossible because you need at least 30 minutes to understand a buyer's style
Late catching is actually better because the buyer has had more time to trust you
There is no meaningful difference; the outcome is the same either way
questions.feedback_correct: Absolutely right—catching pressure behaviors and drops in engagement early gives you the chance to shift and recover rapport before damage is done.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. The timing matters enormously. When you catch a style mismatch early—through a pressure behavior or sudden drop in engagement—you can still shift and recover. Catching it late means you are rebuilding trust you never needed to damage in the first place.

questions.question: If a Driver buyer is sending you mixed signals—more relationship-focused than you would expect—what is the most likely explanation?
choices: They are actually an Amiable, not a Driver, and you misread them
They are testing you to see if you really understand their style
They have an adjacent style (like Expressive) that softens how their primary Driver style shows up
They are uncomfortable and hiding their true preferences to be polite
questions.feedback_correct: Exactly—adjacent styles sit next to the primary style on the grid and modify how the primary shows up; a Driver with an Expressive adjacent will be warmer than a pure Driver.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not that one. The adjacent style is the explanation for mixed signals. A Driver with an Expressive adjacent will still be direct and results-focused, but noticeably warmer and more conversational. This is not a misread—it is a style blend you can observe and adjust to.

questions.question: What is versatility in the context of Social Style Selling, and what is it NOT?
choices: It is being agreeable and flexible in a general sense; it is not about deliberately adjusting your approach
It is deliberately adjusting your communication to reduce friction and help the buyer feel understood; it is not about becoming someone you are not
It is matching the buyer's personality exactly; it is not about keeping any part of your own communication style
It is a personality trait you either have or do not have; it is not something you can develop over time
questions.feedback_correct: Perfect—versatility is a conscious, deliberate adjustment to help the buyer connect with you more easily, not an act of pretending or losing your authenticity.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Not quite. Versatility is a deliberate, learned skill of adjusting your communication approach to match the buyer's style—so they feel understood and rapport builds faster. It is not about changing who you are; it is about removing friction from the relationship.
